key_terms.meaning: The temperature of moist air read by an ordinary dry thermometer; one of the two numbers that fix the state of the air.

Mass of water vapour carried by unit mass of dry air: Y = 0.622 p<sub>w</sub>/(P − p<sub>w</sub>), where p<sub>w</sub> is the water-vapour partial pressure, P the total pressure, and Y is in kg water per kg dry air.
Partial pressure of vapour divided by the saturation vapour pressure at the same dry-bulb temperature: R<sub>H</sub> = 100 p<sub>w</sub>/p<sub>s</sub>, expressed as a percentage.
The temperature to which moist air must be cooled at constant pressure and constant Y before it just becomes saturated; below it, liquid water condenses.
Heat needed to raise 1 kg of dry air plus the vapour it carries by 1 K: c<sub>s</sub> ≈ 1.005 + 1.88 Y, in kJ per (kg dry air · K).

Volume occupied by 1 kg of dry air plus its vapour: v<sub>H</sub> = (1/28.97 + Y/18.02) × 22.414 × T/273.15 at 101.325 kPa, in m³ per kg dry air, with T in kelvin; at another total pressure P multiply by 101.325/P.
Enthalpy of 1 kg dry air plus its vapour referred to 0 °C: H ≈ c<sub>s</sub> (t − 0) + 2500 Y, in kJ per kg dry air, where 2500 kJ/kg is the latent heat of vaporisation at 0 °C.
A graph of Y against dry-bulb temperature carrying constant relative humidity, dew-point, wet-bulb and enthalpy lines, so that two known properties fix the state.
The steady temperature reached by air that is contacted with water in an insulated saturator until it leaves saturated, the water being recirculated and its temperature taken as constant.
The temperature shown by a thermometer whose bulb is wrapped in a wet wick and exposed to an air stream; for air–water it equals the adiabatic saturation temperature.

For air–water, h<sub>c</sub>/(k<sub>Y</sub> c<sub>s</sub>) ≈ 1, where h<sub>c</sub> is the heat-transfer coefficient in W/(m²·K) and k<sub>Y</sub> the mass-transfer coefficient in kg/(m²·s·ΔY); this is why wet-bulb and adiabatic saturation temperatures coincide.
A chamber in which water is sprayed into the air stream, used to humidify, dehumidify, cool or clean the air depending on the water temperature.
A device in which warm water falls through rising air and is cooled mainly by evaporation of a small part of the water, with the rest cooled by the resulting loss of sensible heat.
Range = hot-water temperature − cold-water temperature; approach = cold-water temperature − inlet-air wet-bulb temperature, both in °C.

The dimensionless size number of a cooling tower: KaV/L = c<sub>p</sub> ∫ dT/(h* − h) taken from the cold-water to the hot-water temperature, where c<sub>p</sub> = 4.187 kJ/(kg·K), h* is the enthalpy of saturated air at the water temperature and h the enthalpy of the bulk air, both in kJ per kg dry air.
The moisture content of a solid in equilibrium with air of a given humidity and temperature, in kg water per kg dry solid; the solid neither gains nor loses water at this point.
The average moisture content at which the constant-rate drying period ends and the falling-rate period begins, in kg water per kg dry solid.
Drying in which the hot air is forced through a bed of granular solid rather than across its surface, so the air picks up moisture and cools as it climbs the bed.
A slightly inclined rotating cylinder in which wet solid tumbles along the axis while hot air flows through it, used for free-flowing granular solids in continuous operation.

takeaways: Two numbers, the dry-bulb temperature and the humidity ratio, fix every other property of moist air; the rest are computed, not measured.
The psychrometric chart is only those computations drawn once, so a state is located by any two independent properties and everything else is read off.
For air and water the wet-bulb temperature and the adiabatic saturation temperature are the same because the Lewis relation holds.
Humidifying air with recirculated water follows a constant wet-bulb line, so the adiabatic saturation temperature is the lowest temperature that water alone can reach.
Cooling-tower design integrates an enthalpy driving force between the cold-water and hot-water temperatures, and the answer is the tower characteristic.
A solid stops drying at the equilibrium moisture content of the surrounding air, so that water cannot be removed by that air at any longer time.
Drying time is the area under the curve of 1/(drying rate) plotted against moisture content, taken between the starting and ending moistures.
A dryer design is three balances in a row: water, dry air and heat; sizing of the shell follows from the air velocity the solid can tolerate.
bank_note: Long answers in this topic are mostly chart-and-balance numericals (cooling-tower L/G and characteristic, drying times, rotary-dryer balances) plus one comparison of tower or dryer types. Each model answer below works its numbers through to the result.

bank.q: Define absolute humidity, relative humidity, percentage humidity and dew point. Give the unit of each and state how relative humidity and absolute humidity are related. Illustrate with air at 40 °C and 20 % relative humidity at 101.3 kPa, where the vapour pressure of water is 7.38 kPa.
outline: Absolute humidity Y = 0.622 p<sub>A</sub>/(P − p<sub>A</sub>), in kg water per kg dry air
Relative humidity = 100 p<sub>A</sub>/p<sub>AS</sub> at the same dry-bulb temperature
Percentage humidity = 100 Y/Y<sub>s</sub>; not the same as relative humidity
Dew point: cool at constant P and Y until saturated
The relation between Y and RH through p<sub>A</sub>
Numbers for 40 °C and 20 %
answer: Moist air is dry air plus water vapour. The dry air does not change during humidification or drying, so every humidity is counted against 1 kg of dry air.

answer.text: Absolute humidity (humidity ratio) Y is the mass of water vapour carried by 1 kg of dry air. From Dalton's law the mole ratio of vapour to air equals the pressure ratio, and 0.622 = 18.02/28.97 turns it into a mass ratio:
answer.pre:
Y = 0.622 p<sub>A</sub>/(P − p<sub>A</sub>)        kg water/kg dry air

p<sub>A</sub>   partial pressure of water vapour, kPa
P     total pressure, kPa

answer.text: Relative humidity compares the vapour actually present with the most the air could hold at the same temperature:
answer.pre:
RH = 100 p<sub>A</sub>/p<sub>AS</sub>             per cent

p<sub>AS</sub>  vapour pressure of water at the dry-bulb temperature, kPa

answer.text: Percentage humidity compares humidities instead of pressures:
answer.pre:
percentage humidity = 100 Y/Y<sub>s</sub>     per cent
Y<sub>s</sub> = 0.622 p<sub>AS</sub>/(P − p<sub>AS</sub>)

answer: Dew point is the temperature at which the air becomes saturated when cooled at constant total pressure and constant Y. Its unit is °C. It is the saturation temperature of water at the partial pressure p<sub>A</sub>, so it depends on Y and P only, not on the dry-bulb temperature.

Relation between RH and Y. Both depend on p<sub>A</sub>. Eliminating p<sub>A</sub> gives Y = 0.622 (RH/100) p<sub>AS</sub>/[P − (RH/100) p<sub>AS</sub>]. At fixed Y the vapour pressure is fixed, but p<sub>AS</sub> rises steeply with temperature, so warming air lowers its RH without changing Y. RH is therefore not a measure of water content on its own; it needs the temperature with it.
Worked numbers for 40 °C and 20 % RH:

The percentage humidity, 18.9 %, is a little below the RH of 20 %, because the denominator P − p<sub>A</sub> is larger for the actual air than for saturated air. The two are equal only at 0 % and 100 %, and differ most at middle humidities and high temperatures: at 60 °C and 50 % RH the percentage humidity is 44.5 %.

Cooling this air at constant Y to 12.7 °C saturates it; any further cooling condenses water. Heating it to 60 °C leaves Y = 0.00922 and the dew point at 12.7 °C, but the RH falls to 100 × 1.48/19.94 = 7.4 %.

bank.q: What quantities does a psychrometric chart plot on its axes, and which lines are drawn on it? Explain how two known properties locate the state of moist air and how a third property is then read. Show how the chart finds the state when 100 kg/h of dry air at 30 °C and Y = 0.010 mixes with 50 kg/h at 40 °C and Y = 0.020.
outline: Axes: dry-bulb temperature and humidity Y
Lines: saturation, constant RH, wet-bulb (adiabatic saturation), enthalpy scale, humid volume, dew point by horizontal
Two independent properties give one point
Reading the other properties from the point
Processes as paths
Mixing rule with numbers
Chart drawn for one total pressure
answer: The psychrometric (humidity) chart is the humidity calculations drawn once, for air–water at one total pressure, usually 101.3 kPa. The horizontal axis is the dry-bulb temperature T in °C. The vertical axis is the humidity Y in kg water per kg dry air. Each point is one state of moist air.

answer.text: The lines on the chart:

head: Line
What it shows
Shape
rows: below and like the saturation curve
constant Y, hence constant dew point
air cooling as it evaporates water

answer: Locating a state. Any two independent properties fix one point. With dry bulb and wet bulb, go up the vertical line of the dry bulb until it meets the wet-bulb line that starts on the saturation curve at the wet-bulb temperature. With dry bulb and dew point, go across from the saturation curve at the dew point to the dry-bulb line. Dew point and Y are not independent, because each fixes the other.

Reading a third property. From the point, Y is read on the side scale; the dew point by moving horizontally left to the saturation curve; the RH from the nearest RH curve; the wet bulb by following the wet-bulb line up to saturation; the enthalpy from its own scale; the humid volume by interpolating between its lines.
Processes are paths: heating and sensible cooling are horizontal; adiabatic humidification runs up a wet-bulb line; cooling below the dew point follows the saturation curve down.

answer.text: Mixing. Dry air and water are conserved, so the mixture lies on the straight line joining the two states. Worked numbers:

answer: On the chart the point lies one-third of the way from A to B, the ratio 50/150, because it sits closer to the larger stream. Since the enthalpy lines are not quite parallel, the straight-line rule is exact for Y and enthalpy and very nearly so for T.
The chart is valid for one total pressure. At 2 atm or in a vacuum dryer the same Y gives a different p<sub>A</sub>, so the RH and wet-bulb lines move; the equations must then be used directly.

bank.q: Explain the adiabatic saturation process and show that for the air–water system the wet-bulb temperature equals the adiabatic saturation temperature. State the assumption used, and find both temperatures for air at 40 °C with Y = 0.0092 kg/kg dry air.
outline: Insulated saturator, recirculated water, air leaves saturated at T<sub>as</sub>
Enthalpy balance: sensible heat lost = latent heat to evaporate
Adiabatic saturation line Y = Y<sub>as</sub> − (c<sub>s</sub>/λ<sub>as</sub>)(T − T<sub>as</sub>)
Wet-bulb: convection in, evaporation out, steady state
Lewis relation h<sub>c</sub>/(k<sub>Y</sub> c<sub>s</sub>) ≈ 1 makes the two equations identical
Assumptions
Trial solution for 40 °C and 0.0092
answer: An adiabatic saturator is a long, insulated chamber in which air flows over or through a spray of water. The water is recirculated and no make-up heat is added, so the water settles at a steady temperature. Air enters at dry bulb T and humidity Y and leaves saturated at the adiabatic saturation temperature T<sub>as</sub>, with humidity Y<sub>as</sub> = Y<sub>s</sub>(T<sub>as</sub>). Make-up water enters at T<sub>as</sub>.

answer.text: Enthalpy balance per kg dry air, with the reference at T<sub>as</sub>: the air gives up sensible heat c<sub>s</sub>(T − T<sub>as</sub>), and this evaporates (Y<sub>as</sub> − Y) kg of water at T<sub>as</sub>:
answer.pre:
c<sub>s</sub> (T − T<sub>as</sub>) = λ<sub>as</sub> (Y<sub>as</sub> − Y)

Y = Y<sub>as</sub> − (c<sub>s</sub>/λ<sub>as</sub>)(T − T<sub>as</sub>)

c<sub>s</sub>    humid heat of the entering air, kJ/(kg dry air·K)
λ<sub>as</sub>   latent heat of water at T<sub>as</sub>, kJ/kg

answer: On a Y–T chart this is a straight line of slope −c<sub>s</sub>/λ<sub>as</sub>, about −0.00042 kg/kg per K for air–water. Every air state on the line has the same T<sub>as</sub>.

answer.text: Wet-bulb thermometer. A wick on a thermometer bulb is kept wet in a fast air stream. The wick cools until the heat convected to it just supplies the latent heat of the water evaporating from it. At steady state, per m² of wick:
answer.pre:
h<sub>c</sub> (T − T<sub>w</sub>) = k<sub>Y</sub> λ<sub>w</sub> (Y<sub>w</sub> − Y)

Y = Y<sub>w</sub> − [h<sub>c</sub>/(k<sub>Y</sub> λ<sub>w</sub>)](T − T<sub>w</sub>)

h<sub>c</sub>   convective heat-transfer coefficient, W/(m²·K)
k<sub>Y</sub>   mass-transfer coefficient, kg/(m²·s·unit ΔY)
Y<sub>w</sub>   saturation humidity at T<sub>w</sub>

answer: The two lines have the same form. They coincide when h<sub>c</sub>/k<sub>Y</sub> = c<sub>s</sub>, that is when the Lewis number ratio h<sub>c</sub>/(k<sub>Y</sub> c<sub>s</sub>) equals 1. For air–water this ratio is close to 1 (about 0.95 to 1.0 in the usual range of air speed), so T<sub>w</sub> ≈ T<sub>as</sub> and the chart carries one family of lines for both. For air–toluene or other organic vapours the ratio is near 1.8, and the wet bulb lies well above the adiabatic saturation temperature.

Assumptions: the Lewis relation holds; radiation to the wick and conduction along the thermometer stem are negligible; air speed is above about 3 m/s; the wick is fully wet with pure water; and the saturator is long enough for the air to reach saturation.

answer.text: Trial solution for T = 40 °C and Y = 0.0092 (c<sub>s</sub> = 1.005 + 1.88 × 0.0092 = 1.022 kJ/(kg·K), λ ≈ 2450 kJ/kg):

answer: So T<sub>as</sub> = T<sub>w</sub> ≈ 22 °C. The air leaving the saturator has Y = 0.0167, so each kg of dry air picks up 0.0167 − 0.0092 = 0.0075 kg of water and cools by 18 K. Check by energy: 1.022 × 18 = 18.4 kJ of sensible heat, and 0.0075 × 2450 = 18.4 kJ of latent heat.
The practical result is that two thermometer readings, dry bulb and wet bulb, give the humidity of air directly, and the wet bulb is the lowest temperature that evaporation of water alone can reach.

bank.q: Distinguish bound, unbound, free and equilibrium moisture in a wet solid. Explain why free moisture is easy to remove but bound moisture may not be removable at all by the given air. Illustrate with 100 kg of wet solid at 30 % moisture (wet basis) dried in air at 40 % RH, where X* = 0.10 kg/kg dry solid.
outline: Moisture on a dry basis, X = kg water per kg dry solid
Bound: vapour pressure below that of pure water
Unbound: behaves like free liquid water
Equilibrium X* set by the air temperature and RH
Free = X − X*
Why bound moisture may stay
Numbers for the 100 kg sample
answer: Drying problems count water on a dry basis, X = kg water per kg dry solid, because the dry solid does not change. A wet-basis fraction w converts by X = w/(1 − w).

answer.text: The four kinds of moisture:

head: Term
Meaning
Vapour pressure
rows: held in cell walls, fine capillaries or by sorption on surfaces
below that of pure water at the same T
liquid in large pores, beyond the bound amount
equal to that of pure water
the moisture the solid holds with air of given T and RH; no net gain or loss
equal to the partial pressure in the air
X − X*, the part that this air can remove

answer: Free moisture is easy to remove while it includes unbound water: that water evaporates as from an open surface, at the constant drying rate set by the air. As drying proceeds into bound water, its vapour pressure falls below that of pure water, the driving force shrinks and the rate falls.

Bound moisture may not be removable at all. When the vapour pressure of the bound water falls to the partial pressure of water in the air, the solid has reached X*, and drying stops however long it continues. Removing more needs drier air (lower RH) or hotter air, which lowers X* at a given RH. Some bound water is never removed at ordinary conditions.

answer.text: Numbers for the sample (X* = 0.10 at 40 % RH):

answer: X* is measured by holding small weighed samples over saturated salt solutions of known RH at the dryer temperature until their mass stops changing; X* plotted against RH is the sorption isotherm, and the curve read on drying (desorption) lies above the one read on wetting.

So this air can take the solid only down to 7.0 kg of water, a wet-basis moisture of 7.0/77 = 9.1 %. Air at a lower RH would lower X* and remove more. A non-hygroscopic solid such as sand has X* close to zero at every RH, so almost all of its water is free.

bank.q: A rotary dryer handles 2 tonnes per hour of wet solid, reducing moisture from 30 % to 5 % on a wet basis. Ambient air at 25 °C with Y = 0.010 kg/kg dry air is heated to 100 °C, enters the dryer and leaves at 60 °C. Find the water evaporated, the dry-air rate, the heat duty and the drying efficiency, and estimate the shell diameter and length for an air mass velocity of 2 kg/(m²·s). Comment on the design.
outline: Dry solid and dry-basis moistures
Water evaporated
Outlet humidity along the adiabatic line
Dry-air rate from the water balance
Heater duty and efficiency
Diameter from G; length from L/D
Number of heat-transfer units and what it says

answer.text: Step 1. Solids balance. The dry solid passes through unchanged:
answer.pre:
S  = 2000 × (1 − 0.30) = 1400 kg/h
X1 = 0.30/0.70 = 0.4286 kg water/kg dry solid
X2 = 0.05/0.95 = 0.0526 kg water/kg dry solid

answer.text: Step 2. Water evaporated:

W = S (X1 − X2) = 1400 × (0.4286 − 0.0526) = 526 kg/h
Check: feed water 600 kg/h; product 1400/0.95 = 1473.7 kg/h holding 73.7 kg water; 600 − 73.7 = 526 kg/h

The inlet air at 100 °C and Y = 0.010 has a wet-bulb (adiabatic saturation) temperature of about 35.4 °C, where λ = 2417 kJ/kg; c<sub>s</sub> = 1.005 + 1.88 × 0.010 = 1.024 kJ/(kg·K).

efficiency = 1.27/2.39 = 0.53, that is 53 %

answer: Comment. N<sub>t</sub> = 0.97 lies below the economical range of about 1.5 to 2.5. The air leaves too hot, so half the heat is wasted and the air flow, and therefore the shell, is very large. Raising the inlet air to 200 °C, with the outlet still at 60 °C, gives Y2 = 0.070, cuts the air to about 8800 kg/h (a 1.25 m shell at the same G), gives N<sub>t</sub> = 2.5 and raises the efficiency to 140/175 = 80 % before shell losses. The limit is what the solid can tolerate at the hot end; with cocurrent flow the wet solid stays near the wet-bulb temperature, which protects it.

answer.text: Results at the stated air temperatures:

answer: The fan handles the outlet air: v<sub>H</sub> at 60 °C and Y = 0.0269 is 0.985 m³/kg dry air, so the exhaust fan must move 8.63 × 0.985 = 8.5 m³/s.

bank.q: Air at 35 °C dry-bulb and 20 % relative humidity is blown through an air washer that recirculates its own spray water. Describe the path of the air on the psychrometric chart, find the lowest temperature the water can reach, and estimate the exit condition and the water used if 5000 kg/h of dry air is treated in a washer that is 80 % effective.
outline: State of the inlet air: p<sub>A</sub>, Y, dew point
Recirculated water settles at the adiabatic saturation temperature
Path: up the wet-bulb line toward saturation
Trial for T<sub>as</sub>
Effectiveness (T<sub>in</sub> − T<sub>out</sub>)/(T<sub>in</sub> − T<sub>as</sub>)
Exit T, Y and RH
Make-up water; NTU; what a chilled spray would do

answer.text: Inlet air. p<sub>AS</sub>(35 °C) = 5.63 kPa.
answer.pre:
p<sub>A</sub> = 0.20 × 5.63 = 1.126 kPa
Y1  = 0.622 × 1.126/(101.3 − 1.126) = 0.00699 kg/kg dry air
dew point = saturation temperature at 1.126 kPa ≈ 8.7 °C
c<sub>s</sub> = 1.005 + 1.88 × 0.00699 = 1.018 kJ/(kg·K)

answer: Path. The spray water is recirculated with no heater or chiller, so it settles at the adiabatic saturation temperature of the incoming air. The air gives sensible heat to evaporate water, and moves up and to the left along its adiabatic saturation (wet-bulb) line. Its enthalpy stays almost constant, its Y rises, its temperature falls, and it heads toward the saturation curve at T<sub>as</sub> but never crosses it.

answer.text: Lowest water temperature. Solve Y1 = Y<sub>s</sub>(T<sub>as</sub>) − (c<sub>s</sub>/λ)(35 − T<sub>as</sub>) by trial (λ ≈ 2456 kJ/kg near 19 °C):

answer: The water settles at about 18.9 °C, and this is the lowest temperature evaporation can give. Saturated air at that temperature holds Y<sub>as</sub> = 0.0137.

answer.text: Exit air for 80 % effectiveness:
answer.pre:
effectiveness = (T<sub>in</sub> − T<sub>out</sub>)/(T<sub>in</sub> − T<sub>as</sub>)
T<sub>out</sub> = 35 − 0.80 × (35 − 18.9) = 22.1 °C
Y<sub>out</sub> = Y1 + c<sub>s</sub> (35 − 22.1)/λ = 0.00699 + 1.018 × 12.9/2456 = 0.0123 kg/kg dry air

answer: At 22.1 °C, p<sub>AS</sub> = 2.67 kPa and p<sub>A</sub> = 0.0123 × 101.3/0.6343 = 1.97 kPa, so the exit RH is about 74 %. Check: the enthalpy is 53.1 kJ/kg dry air at the inlet and 53.6 at the outlet, nearly equal as the path demands; the small rise is the enthalpy of the water evaporated.

answer.text: Water used:

answer: This is the make-up the basin needs, plus any drift and bleed-off to keep salts from building up in the recirculated water.

answer.text: Transfer units. For the adiabatic case:
answer.pre:
NTU = ln[(T<sub>in</sub> − T<sub>as</sub>)/(T<sub>out</sub> − T<sub>as</sub>)] = ln[1/(1 − 0.80)] = ln 5 = 1.61
90 % effectiveness would need ln 10 = 2.30, 95 % needs 3.00

answer: Each extra few per cent of approach to saturation costs a large increase in spray length or packing, which is why washers are designed for 80 to 90 %.

If the spray were chilled below the air dew point of 8.7 °C, the air would move down toward the water state instead, cooling and losing water: that is dehumidification, a different operation, and it needs a refrigeration load. A spray between 8.7 and 18.9 °C cools the air with only a small change in Y.

bank.q: Compare natural-draft, forced-draft and induced-draft cooling towers, and counterflow with crossflow layouts, in terms of air flow, land area, upkeep and effectiveness. Recommend a type for a large coastal power plant and justify the choice.
outline: How each draft is produced
Forced vs induced: recirculation, fan size, icing
Counterflow vs crossflow: driving force, pressure drop, access
Water losses: evaporation, drift, blowdown
Fan power estimate
Recommendation for a large coastal plant
answer: All cooling towers cool water mainly by evaporating a small part of it into air, so all are limited by the entering-air wet bulb. They differ in how the air is moved and in the direction it meets the water.

answer.text: Draft:

head: Type
How air moves
Strengths
Weaknesses
rows: warm, moist air in a tall shell is lighter than outside air; chimney effect
no fan power, no fan upkeep, very large single units
high capital cost, large land area, poor control of approach, needs a large range
fan at the base blows air in
fan in cool dry air, easy to reach, vibration-free base
slow exhaust can be drawn back in (recirculation); fan size limited; icing of inlet in cold weather
fan at the top pulls air through
fast exhaust plume avoids recirculation; even air distribution; compact
fan works in hot humid air, more corrosion of the drive

answer.text: Flow layout:

head: Layout
Contact
Effect
rows: the coldest water meets the driest air, so the enthalpy driving force is used best and a smaller fill volume gives a given approach
air moves horizontally across falling water
lower air pressure drop and pumping head, easy access to the distribution basins, but a larger fill for the same duty

answer: Effectiveness is judged by the approach that a given fill volume can reach. A smaller approach needs a much larger tower characteristic: from the Merkel integral, the driving force h* − h at the cold end shrinks as the cold water nears the wet bulb.

answer.text: A sense of the fan power. A mechanical tower cell circulating 100 kg/s of water at L/G = 1 moves about 100 kg/s of dry air, about 90 m³/s. With a fan pressure rise of 150 Pa and fan efficiency 0.70:
answer.pre: P = Q Δp/η = 90 × 150/0.70 = 19.3 kW per cell

answer: A large plant needs dozens of such cells, so fan power becomes a few megawatts that a natural-draft tower does not use.

answer.text: Water losses, for a 10 K range with most heat removed by evaporation:
answer.pre:
E ≈ L c<sub>p</sub> ΔT/λ = 4.187 × 10/2410 ≈ 1.7 % of circulation (an upper bound)
Blowdown at 5 cycles of concentration: B = E/(N − 1) = 1.7/4 ≈ 0.43 %

answer: Drift is held below about 0.01 % of circulation by drift eliminators in either type.

Recommendation for a large coastal power plant. A natural-draft counterflow hyperbolic tower suits a base-load plant of several hundred megawatts: the heat load is steady, the range is large (around 10 K), the land is usually available, and saving fan power over decades outweighs the capital cost. Seawater or brackish make-up needs corrosion-resistant fill and concrete, and a limit on cycles of concentration. Where land is short, the plant cycles its load, or a close approach is needed, an induced-draft counterflow mechanical tower is the better choice; crossflow suits smaller plants where low pumping head and easy maintenance matter more than fill volume.
Environmental points: the visible plume, salt drift from seawater towers onto nearby land, noise from fans, and the make-up water drawn.

bank.q: A heat-sensitive granular solid must be dried from a high moisture content to a low one. Compare tray, tunnel, rotary and fluidized-bed dryers on contact time, uniformity, dust, and suitability for heat-sensitive solids, and choose one with justification.
outline: What makes a solid heat-sensitive: product temperature, not air temperature
Tray, tunnel, rotary, fluidized bed compared
Wet-bulb protection during the constant-rate period
Falling-rate period controls the product temperature
Choice and conditions
answer: For a heat-sensitive solid what matters is the temperature of the solid, and for how long. While the surface is wet (the constant-rate period) the solid stays near the wet-bulb temperature of the air. Air at 120 °C with Y = 0.010 has a wet bulb of only about 38 °C, so even hot air is safe at first. Danger comes in the falling-rate period, when the surface dries and its temperature climbs toward the air temperature. A good dryer for such a solid gives every particle the same short exposure and lets the air temperature be lowered as the solid dries.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Dryer
Contact time
Uniformity
Dust
Heat-sensitive solids
rows: poor: top layers dry first, corners differ
good at low temperature, but slow and labour-heavy; vacuum trays for the most sensitive
fair; air can be staged hotter at the wet end, cooler at the dry end
fair; spread of residence times in the shell
only cocurrent, where the hottest gas meets the wettest solid; long hold-up at the hot end is risky
excellent: the bed is well mixed at one temperature
moderate; fines carried out, cyclone needed
very good: bed temperature is set and controlled closely

answer: Analysis. The tray and tunnel dryers are gentle but slow, and their thick layers dry unevenly, so the top layer may overheat while the bottom is still wet. The rotary dryer handles large tonnage cheaply, but its spread of residence times means some particles stay far longer than the average, and attrition makes dust. The fluidized bed mixes particles so well that the whole bed sits at one temperature, a little above the outlet-air wet bulb while free moisture remains, and that temperature can be held below the limit of the solid. Heat and mass transfer to suspended particles are fast, so contact times are short.

Choice. A fluidized-bed dryer, provided the granules are free-flowing, of fairly narrow size range (very roughly 0.05 to 2 mm) and not sticky when wet. For a high initial moisture, a two-stage arrangement works well: a first stage with hotter air removes the free water while the solid is protected at the wet bulb, and a second stage with cooler air (or a plug-flow bed) finishes the falling-rate period without overheating. A batch fluid bed is common for pharmaceutical granules.

If the solid is sticky at high moisture, back-mixing in a fluid bed with dry product is used, or a tray or vacuum dryer takes over. For large tonnage of a moderately sensitive mineral, a cocurrent rotary dryer remains the economical choice.

Design point: since the falling-rate period controls both the time and the product temperature, the test drying curve of the solid, not the dryer catalogue, fixes the second-stage air temperature and the residence time.

bank.q: Examine the assumptions behind the Lewis relation and hence the wet-bulb thermometer. Under what conditions does the wet-bulb reading become unreliable, and what corrections or precautions are used?
outline: Wet-bulb balance h<sub>c</sub>(T − T<sub>w</sub>) = k<sub>Y</sub> λ<sub>w</sub> (Y<sub>w</sub> − Y)
Lewis relation h<sub>c</sub>/(k<sub>Y</sub> c<sub>s</sub>) ≈ 1 and why it holds for air–water
Other gas–vapour pairs
Radiation, conduction, low air speed
Near saturation: small depression, large error
Precautions: aspirated psychrometer, shield, clean wick
Numbers showing the sensitivity

answer.text: The wet-bulb thermometer gives humidity through its steady-state balance:
answer.pre:
h<sub>c</sub> (T − T<sub>w</sub>) = k<sub>Y</sub> λ<sub>w</sub> (Y<sub>w</sub> − Y)
Y = Y<sub>w</sub> − [h<sub>c</sub>/(k<sub>Y</sub> λ<sub>w</sub>)](T − T<sub>w</sub>)

answer: To use the same line as the adiabatic saturator, Y = Y<sub>as</sub> − (c<sub>s</sub>/λ)(T − T<sub>as</sub>), the ratio h<sub>c</sub>/k<sub>Y</sub> must equal the humid heat c<sub>s</sub>. This is the Lewis relation, h<sub>c</sub>/(k<sub>Y</sub> c<sub>s</sub>) ≈ 1. It rests on the heat-and-mass-transfer analogy: h<sub>c</sub>/(k<sub>Y</sub> c<sub>s</sub>) = (Sc/Pr)<sup>2/3</sup> = Le<sup>2/3</sup>. For water vapour in air, Sc ≈ 0.60 and Pr ≈ 0.71, so the ratio is about 0.9 to 1.0. That near-coincidence is a property of water and air only; for toluene or benzene in air the ratio is near 1.8, and the wet bulb is well above the adiabatic saturation temperature.
Assumptions and where they fail:

head: Assumption
Failure
Effect on reading
rows: heat reaches the wick by convection only
radiation from warm walls or sun
conduction from the warm thermometer stem
air speed high enough (above about 3 m/s)
radiation becomes a large share; reading too high
wick fully wet with pure water
dry patches, dirty wick, dissolved salts
reading drifts toward the dry bulb
the wet bulb no longer equals T<sub>as</sub>

answer.text: Size of the radiation error. A wick at 300 K exchanging radiation with surroundings has a radiative coefficient

answer: In still air the convective coefficient is only about 5 to 10 W/(m²·K), so radiation adds as much heat as convection and the reading may be several degrees high. At 3 to 5 m/s, h<sub>c</sub> is around 30 to 50 W/(m²·K) and the error falls to a fraction of a degree. That is why the sling and aspirated psychrometers move the air past the wick.

Sensitivity. For air at 40 °C dry bulb, a wet bulb of 25.0 °C gives Y = 0.0138 kg/kg dry air, while 24.5 °C gives 0.0129 and 25.5 °C gives 0.0146: a reading error of half a degree changes Y by about 6 %.

Near saturation the depression T − T<sub>w</sub> is small, so the same half-degree error is a large fraction of it. At 30 °C a wet bulb of 29 °C gives Y = 0.0252, and 28.5 °C gives 0.0242, while saturated air holds 0.0272; the relative humidity can be wrong by several points. Dew-point hygrometers or capacitive sensors are better there.

Precautions and corrections: use an aspirated (Assmann-type) or sling psychrometer with air speed above 3 m/s; shield the wet bulb from radiation; keep a clean wick wetted with distilled water and wait for a steady reading; read well away from the stem conduction path; use the psychrometric equation with the measured pressure if the pressure is not 1 atm; and for organic vapours use the measured psychrometric ratio, not 1.

bank.q: Explain what happens inside a deep bed during through-circulation drying: how the air temperature and humidity change as the air climbs, how the drying zone travels, and what this does to the total drying time compared with cross-circulation. Use a bed of 100 kg dry solid dried from X = 0.25 to 0.05 by 500 kg/h of air entering at 60 °C with Y = 0.010.
outline: Air cools along its adiabatic line as it climbs
Exit state from the number of heat-transfer units of the bed
Limit: adiabatic saturation of the inlet air
Three zones and the moving drying front
Time set by the last layer
Comparison with cross-circulation
Numbers for the bed
answer: In through-circulation the air is forced up through a bed of granular solid on a perforated floor. In each thin layer the air gives sensible heat to evaporate water and takes the vapour away. While the particles are wet it moves along its adiabatic saturation line, cooling and gaining humidity, so each layer sees cooler, wetter air than the one below.

answer.text: For the inlet air (60 °C, Y = 0.010): T<sub>as</sub> = 27.6 °C, Y<sub>as</sub> = 0.0236, c<sub>s</sub> = 1.024 kJ/(kg·K), λ = 2435 kJ/kg. With a wet bed of depth z the air temperature falls exponentially toward T<sub>as</sub>:
answer.pre:
(T2 − T<sub>as</sub>)/(T1 − T<sub>as</sub>) = exp(−N),   N = h a z/(G c<sub>s</sub>)
Y2 = Y1 + c<sub>s</sub> (T1 − T2)/λ

answer.text: Exit air and the time it would give if the whole bed stayed wet (water to remove 100 × 0.20 = 20 kg):

answer: A bed of two or three units already brings the air close to saturation. Beyond that, more depth adds pressure drop but hardly any pickup. The absolute limit is Y<sub>as</sub>: the bed cannot dry in less than 20/[500 × (0.0236 − 0.010)] = 2.9 h with this air.

Zones and the moving front. At the start the whole bed is wet. The bottom layers meet the hottest, driest air and dry first, down to the equilibrium moisture of that air. Above them is a drying zone, a few bed units deep, where the air does its cooling and humidifying. Above that the solid is still wet and only warms to the wet bulb, since air reaching it is already almost saturated. As drying proceeds the drying zone moves upward like a front. For most of the run the exit air stays near T<sub>as</sub> and Y<sub>as</sub>, and the bed dries at almost the maximum possible rate.

The drying time is set by the last layer to dry, at the top. Near the end the front reaches the top, the exit air temperature rises and the exit humidity falls; the bottom has been at the inlet air temperature for a long time, so a heat-sensitive solid must be judged by the bottom layer, not the average. Reversing the air direction part way through evens out the moisture.

Comparison with cross-circulation. In cross-circulation the air passes over the tray surface, touching only the top face of the layer; the water must move by capillary flow and diffusion to that face. Through-circulation puts every particle in contact with the air, so the area per kg of solid is many times larger, the external heat- and mass-transfer coefficients are higher, and the falling-rate period, controlled by internal diffusion over a particle radius rather than a bed depth, is much shorter. Through-circulation drying times are typically several times shorter for granular, pelleted or extruded solids.

The cost is pressure drop: the fan must push air through the bed, and the drop rises with depth, air velocity and fines. Pastes and fine powders that would pack or blow away cannot be dried this way unless they are first formed into extrudates or granules.

For the stated bed, if it provides about 2 units the air leaves near 32 °C with Y ≈ 0.022 and the run takes about 3.3 to 3.4 h, close to the 2.9 h minimum; a cross-circulation tray dryer on the same air would take several times longer.

glossary.def: The general term for the water vapour present in a gas, measured in several ways such as absolute humidity or relative humidity.
The humidity ratio of air that is saturated with water vapour at the given dry-bulb temperature.
One hundred times the ratio of the actual humidity ratio to the saturation humidity ratio at the same dry-bulb temperature.
One hundred times the ratio of the actual water-vapour partial pressure to the saturation vapour pressure at the same temperature.
Moles of water vapour per mole of vapour-free gas, which equals p<sub>w</sub>/(P − p<sub>w</sub>).
Any operation that increases the water-vapour content of a gas stream.
Any operation that removes water vapour from a gas stream, by cooling below the dew point, absorption or adsorption.
A dehumidification method in which the gas is cooled so that water condenses out, leaving a saturated gas at the lower temperature.
Dehumidification in which the gas contacts a hygroscopic liquid such as lithium chloride solution or glycol, which takes up water.
Dehumidification in which water vapour is held on the surface of a solid such as silica gel or activated alumina.
A humidification method in which live steam is sparged into the air; both the humidity and the temperature rise.
A device in which air passes over a large wetted surface, picking up water vapour without any spray or liquid droplets.
Water added to a cooling tower or washer to replace evaporation, drift and blowdown losses.
Fine water droplets carried out of a cooling tower by the air stream, removed by drift eliminators.
The deliberate purging of circulating water to keep dissolved solids below a limit that would cause scaling.
The difference between the dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures; it measures how much the air can still take up by evaporation.
The removal of a volatile liquid, usually water, from a wet solid by evaporation into a gas stream.
Water held in the larger pores of a solid whose vapour pressure equals that of free water at the same temperature.
Water held inside the solid by chemical or cellular binding, whose vapour pressure is lower than that of free water.
A plot of the drying rate, in kg water per (m²·h), against the moisture content, showing the warming-up, constant-rate and falling-rate periods.
The drying stage in which the solid surface stays wet and the drying rate stays fixed by the external heat and mass transfer.
The drying stage in which the surface is no longer fully wet and the drying rate drops, controlled by the movement of moisture inside the solid.
A continuous dryer in which trucks or trays of solid move through a long chamber against a stream of hot air.
A dryer in which hot air suspends the particles of solid, giving fast, uniform drying at a nearly constant temperature.
The statement that the heat supplied by the air equals the heat used to evaporate water plus the sensible heat of the solid and the losses.
Removing water vapour by compressing moist air, which raises its vapour partial pressure above the saturation value so water condenses, then cooling it to condense more.
